\begin{frontmatter}
\title{Masking cannot remove what is inside the region of interest: location-dependent shortcut mitigation across dermoscopy, ultrasound and capsule endoscopy}

\begin{abstract}
Medical image classifiers exploit acquisition artifacts---hair, sonographer calipers, intestinal debris---that
correlate with the diagnosis; the standard defence restricts the model to the region of interest (ROI). This defence
depends on where the artifact sits. In pre-registered traps built from real artifacts in four diseases and three
modalities, masking removes an out-of-ROI shortcut but leaves an in-ROI one largely intact (crossover $+0.15$ to $+0.38$
reversed-test AUROC, all Holm-significant; $+0.25$ on new patients). Moving the \emph{same} real artifact across the ROI
boundary of the \emph{same} images reproduces the effect (location interaction
\input{tables/review2_abstract_transplant}). It holds for five masking implementations, falls continuously with the
artifact--ROI overlap, replicates across encoders, fine-tuning and zero-shot vision--language scores, and grows when
images with contradicted labels are removed. A linear-Gaussian account predicted 84 results registered before they
existed (mean absolute error 0.011 AUROC). On unaltered data the harm hides in subgroups: overall AUROC barely changes,
but masking lowers AUROC on shortcut-conflicting cases, on a patient-disjoint thyroid split and on new patients, and
lowers sensitivity among malignant nodules carrying a caliper for a near-benchmark fine-tuned model, in a subgroup
registered in advance, partly even after re-tuning the threshold. Against a registered criterion, no remedy dominates
masking; the closest, a class-conditional mean constraint on the masked features, removes masking's failure in every
cohort and on every set of conflicting cases, at a cost of 0.02 overall AUROC on one external set. Audits of ROI-masked
models should report artifact location and shortcut-conflicting performance. Code, pre-registrations and results are
public.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keyword}
shortcut learning \sep spurious correlation \sep region-of-interest masking \sep artifacts \sep dermoscopy \sep ultrasound \sep capsule endoscopy
\end{keyword}
\end{frontmatter}

\section{Introduction}
Deep classifiers for medical images frequently rely on features that are correlated with the label in the
training distribution but are not evidence of disease \citep{geirhos2020shortcut,degrave2021ai}. In dermoscopy,
surgical skin markings \citep{winkler2019markings} and ruler scale bars \citep{winkler2021scalebars} changed
the melanoma predictions of a market-approved system; in chest radiography, pneumothorax classifiers detect the
chest drain that treats the condition rather than the condition itself
\citep{oakden2020hidden,jimenez2023shortcuts,zech2018variable}. Such correlations are causal in origin---suspicious lesions are
measured and marked, collapsed lungs are drained---so they are present in every retrospectively collected dataset.

The most widely recommended defence is to restrict the classifier to the region of interest (ROI): segment the
lesion or the lungs and discard the rest of the image. The rationale assumes that the shortcut lives in the
background. Rulers, hair, ink and drains do not respect that assumption. When the artifact overlaps the ROI,
masking cannot remove it; it removes everything \emph{else}. We ask whether the effect of masking depends on where
the artifact sits, whether that dependence survives when the artifact is moved while the images stay the same, which
quantity governs it, what it costs on unaltered clinical test data, and what to use instead.

\paragraph{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A location law for ROI masking.} In pre-registered traps built from real artifacts in four diseases and
three imaging modalities, masking removes an out-of-ROI shortcut but leaves an in-ROI one largely intact (Holm-significant
crossovers in 4/4 cohorts). Because Trap~A and Trap~B images differ systematically, we test it on fixed images with a \emph{real-artifact transplant}---the same real artifact pasted inside or
outside the ROI of the same images, with a neutral-tissue paste as paste-edge control---and observationally with
covariate-matched traps; it replicates across three encoder families, three model sizes, end-to-end fine-tuning in all
three cohorts where the network learned the task, and the zero-shot scores of vision--language models; it holds for
five masking implementations, is graded in the real overlap, and grows when images with contradicted labels are
removed (Secs.~\ref{sec:law}, \ref{sec:labels}).
\item \textbf{Mechanism and a closed-form account.} Masking retains an in-ROI artifact while removing competing
evidence, so reliance on it grows; a linear-Gaussian model states when in-ROI masking harms and, fitted to each
model's clean and correlated performance only, matches its held-out reversed-test AUROC far better than simple
reference predictors and predicted 84 results registered before they existed (pre-registered; Secs.~\ref{sec:mech},
\ref{sec:theory}).
\item \textbf{Clinical consequences on unaltered data.} Masking leaves overall AUROC nearly unchanged but lowers it
on shortcut-conflicting cases, on the patient-disjoint official thyroid split and on new patients (ISIC 2019 $\to$ ISIC
2020). For a fine-tuned thyroid model near the published benchmark it lowers sensitivity among malignant nodules that
carry a caliper, in a subgroup registered in advance, and part of that loss survives thresholds re-tuned on the test set
(Sec.~\ref{sec:natural}).
\item \textbf{What to use instead.} A class-conditional mean constraint on the masked features, derived from the law,
removes masking's in-ROI failure in every cohort, including one held out from every choice, and on the
shortcut-conflicting cases of every unaltered test set, and is equal to masking elsewhere except for overall AUROC on one
external set. Against a registered criterion for dominating masking, tested in two rounds on newly generated data and
against published remedies (DFR, JTT, IRM, V-REx, LEACE, SPLINCE, LaMa inpainting) and a documented search,
no remedy dominates; this one fails on one of 42 components. Without artifact labels, an annotation-free mask-then-erase
tool handles overlay-like artifacts (Sec.~\ref{sec:guide}; methods in the supplement).
\item \textbf{Reproducibility.} Pre-registration of every experiment with a registry of commit times, Holm-corrected
primary claims, replication of the original pilot (73/88 numbers), a full rebuild on new hardware that reproduces
every primary crossover within 0.01, artifact labels checked without a clinician against public expert annotations
and two independent automatic labellers, public code, and a CLAIM 2024 checklist.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related work}
\paragraph{Artifacts in dermoscopy} \citet{bissoto2020debiasing} annotated seven artifact types in ISIC images and
showed that debiasing is harder than it looks; \citet{nauta2022uncovering} neutralised coloured calibration patches
by inpainting and retraining---an artifact that a colour rule localises and that lies largely outside the lesion.
Hair occlusion degrades classifiers trained on HAM10000 \citep{wang2024hair}, and removing dermoscopic dark-corner
artifacts is not clearly beneficial, whereas adding synthetic ones to the training set improves classification
\citep{pewton2024dca}; both treat an artifact's presence, not its position relative to the lesion.
MaskMedPaint \citep{maskmedpaint} inpaints regions \emph{outside} the classification-relevant area. None of these
treats artifact location relative to the ROI as a variable.
\paragraph{Ultrasound} In fetal ultrasound, calipers and on-screen text act as shortcuts even for segmentation
\citep{lin2024segshortcut}; we study them for classification in thyroid and ovarian ultrasound, where they lie on
the nodule or tumour.
\paragraph{Chest radiography} Hospital-specific signals limit the generalisation of pneumonia classifiers
\citep{zech2018variable}. Drain-driven pneumothorax shortcuts are documented on NIH-CXR14 and CheXpert
\citep{oakden2020hidden,jimenez2023shortcuts}; recent work localises them to late layers of probed encoders
\citep{pedersen2026probes} and mitigates them by prevalence-equalised recalibration \citep{kina2026prevalence},
which requires the artifact label at test time.
\paragraph{Group robustness and erasure} Reweighting and GroupDRO \citep{sagawa2020groupdro}, last-layer
retraining \citep{kirichenko2023dfr} and linear concept erasure \citep{ravfogel2020inlp,belrose2023leace}
require artifact labels or paired data; erasure from unpaired labels removes label-correlated signal when the
concept is correlated with the label, which is why the mask-then-erase tool we benchmark builds pairs by insertion. Task-preserving linear erasure
(SPLINCE; \citealp{splice2025}) and projection of biased directions in vision--language models \citep{chuang2023debiasing}
are the closest erasure methods; both require concept labels or prompts, whereas our concept subspace is estimated
from synthetic insertions. Random erasing and occlusion augmentation \citep{zhong2020random,fong2019occlusions}
use similar overlays as training noise; in our traps this does not remove the shortcut. Test-time selection
\citep{bissoto2023tts} steers dermoscopy models with user keypoints.
\paragraph{Foundation models} Classifiers trained on frozen foundation-model features inherit shortcut-like
behaviour that pooled multi-institutional evaluation can hide \citep{germani2026aggregation}, and shortcut testing
\citep{brown2023shortcut} probes whether a model's performance gaps stem from encoding a sensitive attribute. We ask where in
the image the shortcut sits and what masking can and cannot remove.

\section{Problem setup and protocol}\label{sec:setup}
Let $Y\in\{0,1\}$ be the diagnosis and $A\in\{0,1\}$ the presence of an artifact. A \emph{trap} trains with
$P(A{=}1\mid Y{=}1)=0.9$ and $P(A{=}1\mid Y{=}0)=0.1$ and tests on a correlated environment with the same rates,
a \emph{reversed} environment with the rates swapped (0.1/0.9), and a clean environment in which the artifact is
independent of the label (real traps: present in half of each class; controlled sweeps: absent). A model
that uses $A$ gains on the correlated test and collapses on the reversed one; the primary metric is reversed-test
AUROC, and clean AUROC measures the cost of a mitigation. The overlap $r=|\mathrm{artifact}\cap\mathrm{ROI}|/|\mathrm{artifact}|$
is the controlled variable. Three designs vary it: \emph{controlled sweeps} paste a synthetic artifact at overlaps
0--100\% on artifact-free images; \emph{real traps} compare images whose real artifact lies inside the ROI
($r\ge0.5$, Trap~A) or outside it ($r<0.1$, Trap~B), each added to one shared artifact-free group; the
\emph{real-artifact transplant} pastes one real artifact instance, cut out with its mask, inside ($r\ge0.95$) or
outside ($r=0$) the ROI of the same artifact-free images. The \emph{location crossover}
$[\text{mask}-\text{ERM}]_{\text{out}}-[\text{mask}-\text{ERM}]_{\text{in}}$ of reversed-test AUROC summarises each
design. Unless stated otherwise backbones are frozen and linear heads are fitted (end-to-end fine-tuning in
Sec.~\ref{sec:replication}); regularisation strength and the decision threshold (balanced accuracy) are selected on
clean validation data only. Uncertainty is a paired bootstrap that resamples training seeds (or cross-validation folds) and test images and
computes AUROC differences inside each cluster; predictions of different models are never pooled into one ROC curve.
Because the seeds of one analysis are evaluated on largely the same test images, the headline claims use a
\emph{crossed} bootstrap that draws one weight per test image shared across all seeds; the per-seed bootstrap of the
original protocol, which resamples images independently within each seed, gives CIs 1.1--2.2 times narrower
(Supplement~S15). Analyses whose predictions were not regenerated (controlled sweeps, the mitigation arms of
Supplement~S8) keep the per-seed CIs. Registration status: the real traps, sweeps and unaltered-data tests were
registered before their results (the 16-test primary family was grouped afterwards); the covariate-matched traps, the
transplant, its paste-edge control and the operating points were designed after the real-trap results and registered
before their own results, and each forms its own Holm family outside the primary family (Supplement~S1). The
analyses added later---masking implementations, overlap dose-response, the external natural test, the prospective
theory test, the label checks, the fine-tuned thyroid model and the threshold re-tuning---were registered in four
further documents, each committed and pushed before its analysis; analyses decided after their data were seen are
labelled exploratory.
Splits are grouped by lesion/patient identifier where published and otherwise by perceptual hash (and frame
blocks); a stricter embedding-based grouping is a sensitivity analysis (Sec.~\ref{sec:leak_emb}).

\section{Discussion and limitations}\label{sec:limits}
\input{sections/discussion}

\section{Conclusion}
ROI masking is not a neutral preprocessing step. Its benefit depends on where the artifact sits: it removes shortcuts
that live outside the ROI and leaves---or amplifies---those that live inside it. Moving the same real artifact across
the ROI boundary of the same images reproduces the effect in all four cohorts, so it is not an artefact of which
images happen to carry in-ROI artifacts; it holds across encoder families and model sizes and, where the network
learns the task, after fine-tuning; a neutral paste
through the same masks behaves similarly, so it is the location of a label-correlated pattern that matters. It follows
from a two-parameter model of signal and artifact strength, which predicted new results before they existed. It holds for
every masking implementation we tried and is graded in the real overlap. On unaltered clinical data the cost falls on
the cases in which the in-ROI artifact points to the wrong diagnosis: it is hidden in the overall AUROC, visible on new
patients, and for a fine-tuned thyroid model part of it survives any re-tuning of the decision threshold. No remedy we
tested dominates masking, but one comes within a single cell. We
recommend that shortcut audits of masked models report artifact location relative to the ROI and evaluate performance
on shortcut-conflicting cases alongside clean and correlated performance, and that, where artifacts may lie inside the
ROI, a class-conditional constraint on the masked features be used instead of masking alone. Code, pre-registrations,
result files and a CLAIM 2024 checklist are public.
